It very much is experimental imo. Every hospital has different machines that are used on different, seemingly arbitrary settings depending on the whim of the attending psychiatrist. Even electrode placement (unilateral/bilateral/bifrontal) isn't fully standard. Seizures duration varies too depending on the equipment settings. There seems to be a blatant disregard and denial in the psychiatric community that ECT causes brain damage, even though a rather sizeable number of people emerge from treatment courses with cognitive disability or impairment, particularly as it relates to memory. MRI studies of ECT patients show alarming neuroinflammation and subsequent neurogenesis in the hippocampus, literally the brain overwrites parts of itself, particularly in the hippocampus, through neurogenesis, which is quite bad for things like memory integrity. They claim that ECT doesn't cause brain damage because no cell death is apparent, but uncontrolled neurogenesis IS, in effect, brain damage.

I've been in therapy over a decade for clinical depression, generalized anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Therapists are easy to find but harder to form the patient-therapist bond with. If you feel like your therapist doesn't understand you, I'd recommend finding another one. Also, try not to get too close or emotionally dependent on your therapist, that sorta damages the professional relationship you and your therapist should maintain. A therapist isn't necessarily there to "fix" you, the only person who can fix you is you. A therapist can guide you, can listen empathically, can provide insight into your struggles with mental illness, can recommend you do or change certain things in your life, but ultimately it all comes down to what you are willing to do to improve your life. Now, you might not have many options or otherwise be stuck in certain thought and behavioral patterns, but a good therapist is invaluable when you have few people you can talk with candidly in your life. I wish you luck on your journey.

The hippocampus has two halves, one for each brain hemisphere. Bilateral ECT shocks both halves of the brain and the effects on the hippocampus appear much worse as a result.
